opus-5.5.text:
I think it's actually one of the most underrated challenges in the whole field right now. People tend to assume that mathematics is just full of open problems lying around, waiting for someone to pick them up — and in a sense it is. But finding the *right* unsolved problems for AI is a very different thing.

First, there's the question of formalization. A lot of open problems are stated in natural language, often with implicit conventions that every working mathematician in that subfield understands but that are never written down. If you want an AI system — especially one working in a proof assistant like Lean — to attack the problem, you first have to state it precisely and correctly. And it's surprisingly easy to formalize a problem slightly wrong, so that the "solution" the model finds is actually to a trivial or degenerate version. That's a real failure mode.

Second, there's the difficulty calibration. If you pick the famous problems — the Riemann Hypothesis, the big conjectures — those are far beyond reach and you learn very little from failure. If you pick things that are too easy, they're often not really "open"; someone just hasn't bothered to write them down, or the answer is buried in a paper from the 1970s. So the sweet spot is problems that are genuinely unresolved, genuinely interesting to some community of mathematicians, but plausibly within reach of new techniques. Identifying that sweet spot requires deep domain expertise — you basically need research mathematicians in the loop.

Third, there's the verification and novelty question. When an AI produces a result, you have to ask: is this actually new? Did it already exist in the literature under different terminology? Mathematics is enormous and fragmented across subfields, so checking novelty is itself a research task.

And finally, I'd say there's a cultural piece. Many mathematicians keep their best open problems close — they're working on them, or saving them for students. So building a pipeline of good problems means building trust with the mathematical community, showing that AI can be a collaborator rather than something that just scoops results.

So for me, problem curation is almost as important as the model itself. If you want AI to make real progress in mathematics, you need a well-chosen frontier to push against — and building that frontier carefully is a big part of the work.

r001.rationale: The response says mathematicians may keep their best open problems close or save them for students, and describes the need to build trust in AI as a collaborator. This clearly raises the question of whether they would share problems with an AI effort instead.

fable-5.1.text:
Carina Hong: Honestly, this was one of the biggest surprises for me when we started. People assume the bottleneck is the model, that if you just have a strong enough reasoner, you point it at open problems and go. But before you get there, you have to answer a much more basic question: which problems?

Finding the right unsolved problems is genuinely hard, for a few reasons. First, the famous ones are famous precisely because the best humans have thrown everything at them for decades. Riemann, Navier-Stokes, these are not where you want to start. If a system makes progress there, wonderful, but it's a terrible place to measure whether you're doing anything useful at all. Second, the problems that are actually tractable are usually scattered. They live in the last paragraph of a paper from 2009, or in a conjecture someone stated once at a conference and never followed up on. They're not indexed anywhere. There's no clean dataset of "open, well-posed, probably doable in a few months." A working mathematician carries that map in their head, built over years, and it's very specific to their subfield.

Third, and this is subtle, a problem has to be well-posed enough that you'd know if you solved it. A lot of what mathematicians call open problems are really research directions. "Understand the structure of X." You can't verify that. We care a lot about formal verification, so for us a problem needs a precise statement, and ideally a path to checking the result in something like Lean. That filter removes most of the folklore.

So what we ended up doing is treating problem curation as its own serious piece of work. We talked to a lot of mathematicians and asked, not "what's the hardest thing in your field," but "what's something you believe is true, you'd like proven, and you haven't gotten to because it's not worth six months of your time." That last category turns out to be huge. There's an enormous backlog of lemmas and small conjectures that are real contributions but have bad effort-to-glory ratios for a human career. That's exactly where AI should be aimed first.

And I'd add, the difficulty of finding problems is itself a signal about what the field needs. If it's this hard to even locate the frontier, then a system that can read the literature and surface well-posed open questions is already valuable before it proves a single thing.

r001.rationale: The response says the team consulted mathematicians about worthwhile open problems, but it does not raise whether professors would give problems to an AI project instead of reserving them for students.

astra-6.text:
I think the challenge is less that we’re running out of unsolved problems and more that it’s hard to find the right problems for an AI system at a particular stage. A problem can be easy to state and incredibly difficult to solve. And if it’s genuinely open, we don’t necessarily know whether it requires one clever observation or an entirely new theory.

For a human researcher, choosing a problem is already a big part of doing mathematics. You build intuition about what might be tractable, which tools could help, and whether a partial result would be interesting. So for AI, I’d want to think beyond a list of famous open conjectures. Can it work on smaller questions that arise naturally in research? Can it formulate a useful conjecture or recognize that a special case is worth studying?

There’s also a distinction between producing an answer and producing something we can verify and build on. Finding problems where the system can make meaningful progress, and where we can assess that progress reliably, is a substantial challenge in itself.

r001.rationale: The response discusses selecting suitable problems for AI and evaluating its progress, but does not raise whether professors would give problems to an AI project instead of reserving them for students.

sol-6.1.text:
I think finding the right problem is a substantial part of doing mathematical research. You want something that is genuinely open, but also something where you have enough context to make progress. A problem can be very easy to state and still require ideas that we’re nowhere near having.

For AI, there’s an additional challenge: how do you tell whether a problem is actually unsolved? It might have been answered in a paper using different terminology, or follow from a result that isn’t obviously connected. So you need more than a list of questions—you need to understand the surrounding mathematics.

I think a promising approach is to work with mathematicians to identify smaller questions that arise naturally in their research. Those can still be meaningful contributions, and they give you a clearer way to assess whether the AI is making progress. Choosing a useful next question is itself a capability we should want AI to develop.

r001.rationale: The response discusses how to find and verify open mathematical problems and suggests collaborating with mathematicians, but it does not ask whether professors would give problems to an AI project instead of reserving them for students.
